vignette:
He is 41 now, a construction worker who spends most days high above the ground fastening steel, pouring concrete, and moving through noise that would rattle most people. On site, other men describe him as solid and dependable. He arrives early, keeps his tools in order, and rarely complains. He is also known for startling hard when something drops unexpectedly behind him, for going quiet when arguments break out, and for leaving without much explanation if voices become too sharp. He lives alone and has for years. He says he prefers it that way. It is easier, he explains, when no one is in his space and no one asks too many questions.

He grew up in a small apartment with his parents and siblings, where the mood of the household depended almost entirely on his father. As a boy, he learned to read the sounds that came before violence: the front door opening too hard, the scrape of a chair, his mother’s voice turning careful and flat. He remembers nights when he would sit frozen in another room, listening to shouting rise through the walls, then the unmistakable sounds of hitting, breaking, his mother crying out and then trying not to cry out. Sometimes he saw it directly. He remembers standing in a doorway and seeing his father strike his mother across the face so hard that she fell against a table. He remembers the shame of doing nothing, though he was only a child, and the terror that if he moved or spoke, his father would turn on him next. He often gathered his younger siblings into a bedroom and told them to stay quiet. He learned early that noise was dangerous, that anger came fast, and that home was a place where a person had to stay alert.

Even when there was no fight, he never relaxed. He watched his father’s expression, listened for changes in breathing, tracked the level of tension in the apartment the way other children might track weather. At school, teachers described him as distracted. He had trouble following lessons because he was tired from being awake late into the night, waiting for the next eruption. He rarely invited friends over. He began to carry himself like someone expecting impact.

As a teenager, he spent as much time as he could outside the home. He started working young, taking whatever jobs he could find, and eventually moved into construction because it rewarded endurance, toughness, and keeping emotions contained. He liked that the expectations were clear. Lift this, measure that, finish the task. There was relief in physical exhaustion. If he came home with his body aching, sometimes his mind was quieter.

But the past does not stay in the past for him. He says that when he hears a man yelling at a woman—even from another apartment, a parking lot, a television in the next room—his chest tightens instantly. He does not just remember; he feels as if he is back there, small and bracing. His heart pounds, his jaw locks, and his thoughts narrow to escape routes and worst-case outcomes. On one job site, two coworkers began shouting at each other near a stairwell. He dropped what he was carrying and spun around so fast he nearly lost his footing. For the rest of the day he could not settle. He kept replaying their voices in his head, though nothing had happened to him.

Sleep is one of the places the old fear returns most strongly. He dreads it. He falls asleep with the television on or with a fan running because silence makes him too aware of every creak and shift in the building. When he does sleep, he often wakes abruptly, sweating and disoriented, from dreams in which he is again in the apartment hearing his mother being hurt and unable to reach her. Sometimes he wakes already standing, as if his body has decided to flee before he is fully conscious. The next day he goes to work exhausted, irritable, and ashamed that a memory can still control him.

He avoids intimate relationships, though he does not describe himself as uninterested in love. Instead, closeness feels dangerous. He says that when a woman he cares about becomes upset with him, even mildly, he feels panic under the surface. If a conversation begins to sound like conflict, he shuts down or leaves. More than one relationship has ended because he seemed distant, secretive, unreachable. He tells himself he is protecting both people. He cannot bear the idea of becoming like his father, and he cannot tolerate the helplessness he feels when he imagines failing to protect someone he loves.

There is a heaviness he carries about himself. He speaks of his childhood with a kind of harshness, calling himself weak for hiding with his siblings, though he also knows they depended on him. He has long stretches when he feels detached from other people, as if everyone else learned some basic sense of safety that he missed. He keeps mostly to himself, goes to work, comes home, and stays busy with repairs around his apartment. Still, even in ordinary moments, his body remains watchful. He sits facing doors. He scans rooms without realizing it. He notices the tone between couples, the volume of footsteps overhead, the slam of cabinets in neighboring units.

He says he is tired of living as if something terrible is about to happen. Yet that expectation has become so familiar that he does not know who he would be without it. Even now, decades after those nights in childhood, part of him remains in that apartment, listening through the wall, waiting for the next blow.
